content: When handling items contaminated with blood or body fluids, always separate them from other laundry. Use gloves or a plastic bag to avoid direct contact. Do not touch these items with bare hands. Rinse off any blood or body fluids before washing with soap. Instruments that penetrate the skin, such as needles, must be properly sterilized or disposed of after a single use. Equipment that comes into contact with intact skin should be cleaned and disinfected according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Reusing gloves is not recommended. However, if glove reuse is unavoidable due to limited supply, clean and disinfect them thoroughly. Wash gloves with soap and water, then inspect them for damage by inflating them with air, sealing the cuff, and submerging them in clean water to check for leaks. Discard any damaged gloves. Disinfect gloves using a solution of 5% available chlorine (prepared by mixing 90 mL of water with 10 mL of bleach containing 5% chlorine). Allow gloves to dry away from direct sunlight and dust the inside with talcum powder or starch. Note that disinfected gloves are not sterile. Perform a quick check on all incoming patients, including those in the waiting room, to identify any emergency signs. If a woman is in labor, accompany her to an appropriate area and follow the steps for labor, delivery, and immediate postpartum care. If priority signs are present, examine the patient immediately using the relevant antenatal, postpartum, or post-abortion care guidelines. If no emergency or priority signs are detected, invite the patient to wait in the designated area. For emergency care, introduce yourself to the patient, ask for her name, and encourage her companion to stay with her. Explain all procedures, seek permission, and keep the patient informed throughout the process. If the patient is unconscious, communicate with her companion. Maintain privacy during examinations and discussions. If the patient has a baby and the baby is well, ask the companion to care for the baby during the maternal examination and treatment. Follow-up care may be organized by the referral facility or provided through written instructions for the primary care provider. Advise the patient to return for a follow-up visit within two weeks, depending on the severity of the condition. During routine visits, greet the patient, offer her a seat, and introduce yourself. Ask for her name and the baby’s name, if applicable. Inquire about the reason for the visit, whether it is for herself or her baby, and whether it is a scheduled or follow-up visit. If the patient is recently postpartum, assess the baby or ask to see the baby if not present. For antenatal care visits, review the birth plan at the end of the visit. For postpartum visits, examine both the mother and baby using the appropriate guidelines. If the visit is a follow-up within a week, focus on the specific condition requiring follow-up. For follow-ups more than a week after the initial visit, repeat the full assessment as required. During the visit, explain all procedures, seek permission before conducting examinations or tests, and keep the patient informed throughout. Discuss findings with the patient and her partner, if present, while ensuring privacy. At the end of the visit, address any questions the patient may have, summarize key messages, and encourage her to return for routine care or if any concerns arise. Complete the Home-Based Maternal Record (HBMR) and provide the patient with relevant information sheets. For rapid assessment and management (RAM) of women of childbearing age, assess all emergency and priority signs upon arrival and periodically during labor, delivery, and the postpartum period. Provide appropriate treatments and refer the patient to a hospital if necessary. Emergency signs include severe difficulty breathing, central cyanosis, cold and moist skin, weak and rapid pulse, or heavy bleeding. For shock, position the patient on her left side with legs elevated, insert an IV line, and administer fluids rapidly. Keep the patient warm and provide appropriate medications, such as oxytocin or antibiotics, depending on the condition. For vaginal bleeding during late pregnancy or labor, avoid vaginal examinations. Insert an IV line, administer fluids rapidly if bleeding is heavy, and refer the patient urgently to a hospital. If the placenta is not delivered, attempt controlled cord traction or manual removal. If unsuccessful, refer the patient urgently. For postpartum bleeding, massage the uterus until it is firm, administer oxytocin, and empty the bladder. If bleeding persists, check for retained placental fragments or perineal tears and manage accordingly. If bleeding remains uncontrolled, administer additional medications, apply uterine or aortic compression, and refer the patient urgently. Refer the patient urgently to a hospital for further management. Always prioritize the safety and well-being of the patient and her baby, ensuring timely and appropriate care.
